Epigenetics & Imprinting

Updated Oct 9, 2026 Revision 1.0 6 learning objectives

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Define epigenetics, name its main mechanisms and explain how environment changes gene expression without changing DNA sequence.
  2. LO 2Explain genomic imprinting and the four ways an imprinted region can fail.
  3. LO 3Compare Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes by parent of origin, mechanism and presentation.
  4. LO 4Describe Beckwith-Wiedemann (and its mirror, Silver-Russell) and why assisted reproduction raises its risk.
  5. LO 5Sort disorders of the epigenetic machinery into writers, erasers, remodelers and readers, and recognize each syndrome.
  6. LO 6Choose the right test for a suspected imprinting disorder and outline future epigenetic therapies.

MAPBig picture: two kinds of epigenetic disease

LO 1What is epigenetics?

Q1. How is epigenetics defined?
  • Modifications of the DNA or associated proteins, other than the sequence itself, that are heritable through cell division
  • Three properties:
    • Reversible
    • Affected by environment
    • Reset in germ cells
  • Explains why genetically identical MZ twins drift apart in phenotype over time
Analogy — the conductor's notes

DNA is the musical score. Epigenetic marks are the conductor's pencil notes ("skip this part," "play loudly"). Same score, very different performance, and the notes can be erased.

Q2. What are the main epigenetic mechanisms?
MechanismWhat happensEffect
DNA methylationDNMT adds CH₃ (from SAM) to cytosine at CpG → 5-methylcytosineGene OFF (main mechanism in lecture)
Histone acetylationAcetyl groups loosen chromatin; HDAC removes themAcetylation ON; deacetylation OFF
Histone methylationMethyl on lysine/arginineON or OFF depending on residue
Noncoding RNAXIST, H19, KCNQ1OT1Silence genes in cis
Chromatin remodelingRepositions nucleosomes (e.g., CHD7)Changes DNA access

DNA methylation

  • Cytosine + CH₃ (SAM, DNMT) → 5-methylcytosine → OFF
Memory tool

"Methylation mutes, acetylation activates."

Step 1

Normal uses of methylation: X-inactivation (XIST → Barr body), imprinting, tissue-specific silencing. Fragile X: CGG expansion → hypermethylation → FMR1 silenced. HDAC inhibitors include valproate.

Q3. What does the agouti mouse show?

Same genes, different coats

  • Yellow (unmethylated) → brown pseudo-agouti (methylated)
  • Genetically identical mice
  • Mothers fed methyl donors (folate, B12, choline, betaine) → pups with more methylation of the agouti gene → brown, lean
  • Without them → yellow, obese, diabetic
  • Lesson: environment changed phenotype without changing genotype
In-house exam

Expect: identical genotype + different diet/exposure + different phenotype → epigenetics (agouti mouse, MZ twins).

ApplyLO 1 application question

A1MZ twins share a genome, but at 50 only one has a methylation-silenced tumor suppressor gene. What explains this?
Epigenetic drift: environment changes methylation over time; the sequence is unchanged.

LO 2Genomic imprinting

Q1. What is imprinting, and when are imprints reset?
  • Imprinting = parent-of-origin gene expression: one allele is silenced, the other expressed, depending on which parent it came from
  • Marks sit at CpG-rich differentially methylated regions (DMRs), run by imprint control regions (ICRs); ~100 imprinted genes
  • In gametogenesis:
    1. Old imprints are erased
    2. A new imprint is set by the person's own sex: sperm get a paternal pattern, eggs a maternal pattern

Erase → reset by sex

  • A man passes only paternal imprints; a woman only maternal
High yield — the silent-copy rule

Disease can occur even with a normal copy on the other chromosome, because that copy is normally silenced. A mutation on the silent allele does nothing; pass it through the other parent and it becomes the active copy → disease.

Step 1

Parental conflict: the father's genes push growth (IGF2); the mother's restrain it. All-paternal genome (46,XX androgenote) → complete hydatidiform mole.

Q2. What are the four ways an imprinted region fails?
MechanismWhat happensDetect with
1 · DeletionThe active parent's region is missingFISH, microarray, methylation
2 · Uniparental disomy (UPD)Both copies come from one parent; the other parent's active copy is missingMethylation, SNP array, microsatellites
3 · Gene mutationPoint mutation in the active allele (UBE3A, CDKN1C)Sequencing
4 · Imprinting defectICR gains or loses methylation; no DNA changeMethylation only
Trap

A normal karyotype, microarray and exome do not rule out an imprinting disorder: UPD and imprinting defects are invisible to them. Methylation analysis is the first test.

Q3. Why don't imprinting disorders follow Mendelian rules?
  • Penetrance depends on the sex of the transmitting parent
  • Mosaicism (marks set after fertilization) → blood can look normal
  • MZ twins can be discordant

ApplyLO 2 application question

A1A healthy woman inherited a CDKN1C mutation from her father. Her son has Beckwith-Wiedemann. Why is she healthy?
CDKN1C is maternally expressed: silent on her paternal copy, active once she passes it on.

LO 3Prader-Willi and Angelman (15q11–q13)

Q1. What goes wrong in each, and how often by each mechanism?

Top PWS · bottom AS

  • Blue = paternal · red = maternal
MechanismPrader-WilliAngelman
MissingPaternal 15q11–q13 (SNRPN, NDN, MAGEL2, snoRNAs)Maternal UBE3A
Deletion70% (paternal)70% (maternal)
UPD25% (maternal UPD)2% (paternal UPD)
Gene mutation0%20% (UBE3A)
Imprinting defect≤5%≤5%
Memory tool

Prader-Willi = missing Papa. Angelman = missing "Angel mom" (maternal UBE3A). UPD is big in PWS (25%) and tiny in AS (2%); gene mutation only in AS.

Q2. How do they present?

Prader-Willi

  • Neonatal hypotonia, poor suck
  • → hyperphagia, unsafe eating, obesity
  • Moderate ID
  • Hypogenitalism
  • Short stature, small hands/feet
  • Characteristic facies

Angelman

  • Severe ID
  • Minimal–absent speech
  • Stiff, ataxic gait ("happy puppet")
  • Paroxysms of laughter, happy affect
  • Microcephaly, seizures
  • Feeding problems, drooling; sleep disturbance
Step 1

Floppy newborn who becomes a hyperphagic, obese child → PWS. Happy, laughing, ataxic child with seizures → AS. Both: 15q11–q13 deletion on FISH in ~70%.

In-house exam

Know the percentages for each mechanism and which parent is missing. PWS is never caused by a single-gene mutation.

ApplyLO 3 application question

A1A child with PWS features has a normal FISH for 15q11–q13. Most likely mechanism and test?
Maternal UPD15 (25%); confirm with methylation analysis (maternal-only pattern) and SNP/microsatellite studies.

LO 4Beckwith-Wiedemann, Silver-Russell and assisted reproduction

Q1. What does BWS look like?
  • Large for gestational age (macrosomia)
  • Macroglossia
  • Ear pits/creases
  • Omphalocele
  • Hemihypertrophy (one side larger)
  • Neonatal hypoglycemia
  • Cancer risk: Wilms, hepatoblastoma
Memory tool — BWS = "Big"

Big baby, Big tongue, Belly-wall defect, Bigger on one side, Blood sugar low, Bad tumors.

Step 1

Screen for tumors through early childhood: abdominal ultrasound (Wilms) + AFP (hepatoblastoma). WAGR and Denys-Drash are the other Wilms syndromes.

Q2. How does 11p15 control growth?

IC2 (left) and IC1 (right)

  • Orange dot = methylation · blue = CTCF insulator
CenterPaternal (normal)Maternal (normal)
IC1 (H19 / IGF2)Methylated → H19 off → IGF2 on (growth ↑)Unmethylated → H19 on, IGF2 off
IC2 (KCNQ1OT1 / CDKN1C)Unmethylated → KCNQ1OT1 on → CDKN1C offMethylated → CDKN1C on (p57, growth ↓)
Q3. What causes BWS?

Causes of BWS

  • Half = maternal IC2 loses methylation
Mechanism%
Loss of methylation at IC2 (maternal)~50%
Paternal UPD 11p15.5~20%
Unknown~20%
Gain of methylation at IC1 (maternal)~5%
Maternal CDKN1C mutation~5%
Deletion / duplication / translocation<1% each
In-house exam

Most common cause of BWS = loss of methylation of imprinting center 2 on the maternal chromosome 11 (~50%).

Q4. What is Silver-Russell, the mirror of BWS?
  • IUGR/SGA, postnatal growth failure, relatively normal head size
  • Body asymmetry, triangular face, 5th-finger clinodactyly, feeding problems
  • Causes: loss of methylation at IC1 (paternal) (most common); maternal UPD7 (~10%)
Q5. Why does assisted reproduction raise BWS risk?

ART hits the imprint window

  • Ovulation induction and embryo culture overlap imprint setting/maintenance
  • BWS risk after ART: 1 in 4,000 vs 1 in 13,700 in the general population (~3×)
  • Imprints are set during gametogenesis and maintained in the early embryo: exactly when ART manipulates them (ovulation induction, in-vitro culture)
  • Most post-ART BWS = loss of methylation at IC2
  • An example of environment changing epigenetics without changing DNA
In-house exam

IVF baby + LGA + macroglossia + omphalocele + hypoglycemia → BWS; know the 1:4,000 vs 1:13,700 numbers.

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1A newborn conceived by IVF has a large tongue, omphalocele and a glucose of 30 mg/dL. Most likely mechanism, and what follow-up?
BWS, most often IC2 loss of maternal methylation; screen with abdominal ultrasound and AFP.
A2An SGA infant has a triangular face, normal head size and limb asymmetry. Test shows maternal UPD7. Diagnosis?
Silver-Russell syndrome.

LO 5Disorders of the epigenetic machinery

Q1. What are writers, erasers, remodelers and readers?
ClassJobExample genesSyndromes
WritersPut marks on chromatinCREBBP, EP300, NSD1, EZH2, KMT2DSotos, Weaver, Rubinstein-Taybi, Kabuki
ErasersRemove marksHDAC4, HDAC8Townes-Brocks
RemodelersReorganize chromatin → change DNA accessSRCAP, CHD7CHARGE
ReadersRecognize marks → downstream effectsRPS6KA3, MECP2Smith-Magenis, Rett

The epigenetic toolkit

  • Pens write · erasers erase · bulldozer remodels · glasses read
Analogy — editing a manuscript

Writers add sticky notes, erasers peel them off, the remodeler rearranges the pages, and the reader acts on what the notes say.

Trap — terminology

The lecture calls these "imprinting control disorders," but they are Mendelian mutations (mostly de novo AD; Rett XLD) in genome-wide machinery, not parent-of-origin imprinting defects.

Q2. How do I recognize the writer syndromes?
SyndromeKey featuresGene
SotosOvergrowth (large head, baby, hands); low tone; developmental delay; abnormal teeth; facies; behavioral differencesNSD1
WeaverOvergrowth (large baby, tall); low or high tone; mild ID; joint contractures; kyphoscoliosis; abnormal MRIEZH2
Rubinstein-TaybiBroad thumbs and great toes; dislocated patellas, scoliosis; strabismus, cataracts, glaucoma; ear infections; high palate, talon cusps; heart defects 35–40%; undescended testes; constipationCREBBP, EP300
Kabuki"Kabuki" facies (long eyelids, arched eyebrows), persistent fetal finger pads, IQ <80, joint laxity, hypotonia, short stature, heart defects, cleft lip/palate, renal anomalies, hearing lossKMT2D, KDM6A

Rubinstein-Taybi

  • Broad great toe (and thumb)
In-house exam

Broad thumbs and great toes + heart defect → Rubinstein-Taybi, a writer disorder. Gene names are low yield in lecture; the class is what's tested.

Q3. How do I recognize the eraser and remodeler syndromes?

Townes-Brocks (eraser)

  • Imperforate anus
  • Abnormal ear shape
  • Thumb malformation
  • Rarely: kidney, hearing, heart, genital, learning problems
  • Gene: SALL1

CHARGE (remodeler)

  • Need 4 of 7:
  • Coloboma
  • Heart (conotruncal, arch)
  • choanal Atresia
  • growth/mental Retardation
  • Genitourinary (microphallus)
  • Ear (ossicles, Mondini cochlea, deafness)
  • Gene: CHD7

CHARGE ears

  • Cup-shaped, malformed pinnae

Townes-Brocks thumbs

  • Triphalangeal / malformed thumbs
Memory tool

The eraser "rubs out" the anus (Townes-Brocks: anus, ears, thumbs). The bulldozer remodels a whole CHARGE (spell out the letters).

Trap — look-alikes

Imperforate anus + thumb anomaly also fits VACTERL. Townes-Brocks adds the ear malformation; VACTERL adds vertebral, TE fistula, cardiac and limb defects.

Q4. How do I recognize the reader syndromes?

Smith-Magenis

  • Hypotonia, failure to thrive, small
  • Early speech delay; peripheral neuropathy
  • Severe sleep problems
  • Self-injury, impulsivity, "self-hug," "lick and flip"
  • Features coarsen over time
  • Gene: RAI1 (17p11.2 deletion)

Rett

  • Girls: X-linked dominant
  • Normal early development → regression, especially language loss and hand use
  • Hand-wringing; acquired microcephaly
  • Hyperventilation, bruxism, paroxysmal laughing
  • Prolonged QT; scoliosis
  • Gene: MECP2
Step 1

Rett: girl normal until ~6–18 months → regression, hand-wringing, acquired microcephaly, breathing irregularities; MECP2 (methyl-CpG binding reader); usually lethal in males.

In-house exam

Rett and Smith-Magenis are readers; know that Rett is X-linked dominant and affects girls.

Memory tool — sort them

Writers make things big or broad (Sotos, Weaver, RTS thumbs, Kabuki). Readers lose behavior and language (Smith-Magenis self-hug, Rett regression).

ApplyLO 5 application questions

A1A newborn has bilateral coloboma, tetralogy of Fallot, choanal atresia and cup-shaped ears. Which class of epigenetic defect?
Remodeler: CHARGE (CHD7).
A2An 8-year-old hugs herself repeatedly, wakes many times a night and bites her hands. Diagnosis and class?
Smith-Magenis: a reader disorder (RAI1, 17p11.2).

LO 6Diagnosis and future therapy

Q1. How are imprinting disorders diagnosed?
  • Start with methylation at the DMR/ICR: catches deletion, UPD and imprinting defects in one test
  • Tools: methylation-specific MLPA (copy number + methylation together), bisulfite sequencing, methylation-sensitive PCR or restriction enzymes
  • SNP array / microsatellites → distinguishes UPD from deletion; shows parent of origin
  • Sequencing if methylation is normal (UBE3A in AS, CDKN1C in BWS)
  • Multilocus panels: several imprints can be disturbed at once
  • Mosaicism → test another tissue (buccal, skin) if blood is normal
High yield

Order: methylation → (if abnormal) SNP array / FISH to find the mechanism → (if normal and AS suspected) UBE3A sequencing. Mechanism matters for recurrence risk: deletion/UPD <1%; UBE3A mutation in the mother → up to 50%.

Q2. What therapies might come from epigenetics?
  • The "missing" gene is often present but silenced → unsilencing could treat disease
  • Topoisomerase inhibitors unsilenced paternal Ube3a in Angelman mice
  • HDAC inhibitors (valproate, phenylbutyrate, SAHA)
  • Antisense RNAs / microRNAs; CRISPR epigenome editing; patient iPSCs for drug screening
Analogy — the dimmer switch

In Angelman, the paternal UBE3A bulb works; it's just switched off in neurons. Therapy aims to flip the switch rather than replace the bulb.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1Genetically identical mice born to mothers fed folate, B12 and choline are brown and lean; those born to unsupplemented mothers are yellow and obese. What best explains the difference?

Methyl donors → more methylation → agouti silenced; genotype unchanged.

2A hypotonic newborn with poor suck becomes an obese, constantly hungry toddler with small hands and hypogonadism. FISH for 15q11–q13 is normal. Most likely mechanism?

PWS with normal FISH → maternal UPD15 (25%).

3A 4-year-old with severe ID, no words, seizures, a jerky ataxic gait and frequent laughter has normal methylation at 15q11–q13. Next best test?

Normal methylation rules out deletion, UPD and imprinting defect → AS from UBE3A mutation (20%).

4Which is the most common cause of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?

~50%; paternal UPD ~20%.

5A newborn conceived by in-vitro fertilization weighs 4.9 kg and has macroglossia, an omphalocele and ear creases. Which surveillance is indicated?

BWS → Wilms (ultrasound) and hepatoblastoma (AFP).

6The increased risk of Beckwith-Wiedemann after assisted reproduction is best explained by:

ART overlaps the imprint window; risk 1:4,000 vs 1:13,700.

7An SGA infant has postnatal growth failure, a triangular face, relatively large head and body asymmetry. Which finding is most likely?

Silver-Russell: IC1 loss of methylation (paternal) or maternal UPD7 (~10%).

8A child has broad thumbs and great toes, a congenital heart defect, glaucoma and undescended testes. The defective protein is best classified as an epigenetic:

Rubinstein-Taybi: CREBBP/EP300 acetyltransferases (writers).

9A newborn has an imperforate anus, malformed ears and a triphalangeal thumb. Which category of epigenetic disorder?

Townes-Brocks.

10An infant has coloboma, a conotruncal heart defect, bilateral choanal atresia, microphallus and a Mondini cochlea. The mutated gene encodes a:

CHARGE: CHD7 remodeler.

11An 18-month-old girl stops using words she had learned, loses purposeful hand use and repeatedly wrings her hands. Head growth has slowed. ECG shows a long QT. Inheritance?

Rett: MECP2 reader, XLD, affects girls.

12A child's karyotype, chromosomal microarray and exome are all normal, but an imprinting disorder is suspected. Best next test?

UPD and imprinting defects are invisible to sequence and copy-number tests.
